n: The third friend, Zophar, speaks for the first time. He is the harshest of the three.
Should all this talk go unanswered? Should a big talker be proven right just by talking? Zophar dismisses Job’s pain as mere words.

f.g: Literally “a man of lips” — a windbag.

n: Should your empty boasting silence everyone? When you mock, shouldn’t someone shame you?
Zophar summarizes Job’s claim: “My teaching is pure, and I am clean in your sight.” Job did insist on his innocence, but not that he had never sinned at all.

f.g: My teaching or understanding is sound.

n: Zophar wishes God would speak against Job. Ironically, God does speak at the end — and rebukes the friends instead (Job 42:7).
If only God would show you how deep His wisdom is! Then you’d know God is punishing you less than you deserve. This is Zophar’s cruelest line.

f.w: exacteth of thee less than thine iniquity deserveth

n: Can you discover the depths of God by searching? Can you reach the limits of the Almighty? A true principle — God is beyond full human understanding.

f.w: Canst thou by searching find out God?

n: God’s wisdom is higher than the heavens and deeper than the underworld — beyond our reach.

f.g: Hebrew Sheol — the realm of the dead, here meaning the deepest depths.

n: It is longer than the earth and wider than the sea.
If God arrests someone and calls him to judgment, who can stop Him?
God knows deceitful people; when He sees evil, He takes note. Zophar implies God has seen Job’s hidden sins.
A proverb: a foolish person will become wise when a wild donkey is born human — in other words, never. It is an insult aimed at Job.

f.w: born like a wild ass's colt
f.g: A saying: an empty-headed man will gain sense when a wild donkey is born a man.

n: Zophar’s counsel: set your heart right and reach out your hands to God in prayer.
If there is sin in your hand, put it away, and don’t let evil live in your home. Good advice for repentance — though wrongly assuming Job is guilty.
Then you could lift your face without shame, stand firm, and not be afraid.
You would forget your misery, remembering it like water that has flowed away.
Your life would shine brighter than noon; even darkness would become like morning.
You would feel secure because there is hope; you would look around and rest in safety.

f.g: Possibly “look around” or “search” — you would find all safe.

n: You would lie down without fear, and many would come seeking your favor. Indeed, in the end Job does pray for these very friends (Job 42:8-10).

f.w: many shall make suit unto thee

n: But the wicked will lose all hope; their only hope is their last breath. A final warning shot at Job.

f.w: the eyes of the wicked shall fail
f.g: They will look for help in vain.

f.w: the giving up of the ghost
